blk_part_02_who_ate_it_and_why.text: The best-known people who ate fly agaric for its effects lived far to the east, in Siberia. Some people in Europe also ate it as food, but only after boiling it, which removes part of the poison. Europeans learned about the Siberian use from Philip Johan von Strahlenberg, a Swedish army officer. He spent about ten years in Siberia as a prisoner of the Russian army. In 1730, he published a book about what he saw there. It described the Koryak people of Kamchatka, in the far east of Russia, and how they used the mushroom.

blk_part_02_who_ate_it_and_why.text: For the Koryak, the mushroom was part of their beliefs. In one of their myths, the hero Big Raven cannot lift a bag of food. A whale needs it for its journey home to the sea. Then he eats fly agaric, becomes strong enough and lifts the bag. Shamans, people who were believed to speak with spirits, ate it to enter a dream-like state. Many other people in Siberia ate it simply for fun, the way people in other places drink alcohol. One report says that poor Koryak people drank the urine of rich people, who could buy the mushrooms. This worked because a large part of the active chemicals leaves the body in urine.
